lessons.title: Receiving and checking plant material
lessons.html:
Receiving and checking plant material

Florists work with cut flowers, foliage, pot plants and dried material. These are living, fragile and expensive. Every time a stem is handled roughly it can bruise, snap or lose petals. Careful handling from the moment stock arrives keeps quality high and waste low.

When the delivery arrives

  1. Check the delivery against the order: types, colours, number of bunches or stems.
  2. Check the quality:
    • Stems firm and straight, not slimy at the ends.
    • Leaves green and fresh, not yellow or spotted.
    • Flowers at the right stage of opening: not too tight, not fully blown.
    • No pests such as aphids, thrips or snails.
    • No mould (grey fuzz), especially on roses and gerberas.
  3. Write any problems on the delivery note and tell your supervisor before signing.
  4. Move the stock out of the heat into the work area or cool room straight away.

Sorting

  • Sort by type and colour.
  • Grade by quality and length if your shop does so.
  • Put aside damaged stems. Some can be used as short pieces in arrangements; others must be thrown away.
  • Label buckets with the type and the date received. Use the oldest stock first (first in, first out).

Example

A box of roses arrives. Ayanda finds grey mould on two bunches. She takes them out, tells her supervisor and writes it on the delivery note. If they had been put in the cool room with the rest, the mould could have spread to other flowers and the shop would have lost far more stock.

lessons.title: Handling, storing and moving plant material
lessons.html:
Handling, storing and moving

Handling cut flowers

  • Hold bunches by the stems, not the flower heads.
  • Do not squeeze or stack bunches on top of each other.
  • Carry buckets with care; do not swing them.
  • Keep wrapping on delicate flowers until you condition them.
  • Handle one type at a time so stems do not tangle and break.
  • Keep flowers out of sun, wind and heat.

Handling pot plants

  • Lift by the pot, not by the stems or leaves.
  • Check the soil. Water if dry, but do not leave pots standing in water.
  • Place them in good light, as the plant type needs.
  • Remove dead leaves and flowers.

Handling dried and preserved material

  • Keep it dry and out of direct sun, which fades colours.
  • Handle gently; it breaks easily.
  • Store in boxes so dust does not collect.

Storing cut material

  • Keep stock in clean buckets with fresh water in the cool room.
  • Do not overcrowd buckets.
  • Keep fruit and vegetables out of the flower area. They give off ethylene gas that ages flowers.
  • Check stock every day. Remove dying stems.

Moving and delivering

  • Pack arrangements so they cannot tip over: use boxes, crates or holders.
  • Keep the vehicle cool and drive smoothly.
  • Never leave flowers in a hot parked vehicle.

Safety and hygiene

  • Some plants have thorns or irritating sap. Wear gloves and wash hands after work.
  • Some plants are poisonous if eaten. Keep them away from children and pets, and tell customers.
  • Wipe up water spills at once.
  • Lift heavy buckets with bent knees.

Key points

  • Check deliveries for quantity, quality, pests and mould.
  • Sort, label with dates and use oldest stock first.
  • Hold flowers by the stems and pot plants by the pot.
  • Store in clean water, in the cool room, away from fruit.
  • Pack and transport carefully and keep material cool.
